title: Composition

learn.summary: Composition is deciding what goes where in the frame and why — the difference between a rendered study and a picture someone wants to look at. The eye follows values, edges, and lines wherever the artist sends it; good composition is deliberate traffic direction. Cheap insurance: thumbnail every serious drawing before starting it.

do: Before your next finished drawing, produce four postage-stamp thumbnails of different arrangements and pick the strongest — every time, no exceptions, starting this week.

children.title: Focal Point

learn.summary: The focal point is where you want the viewer's eye to land, and you build it with converging tools: highest value contrast, sharpest edges, most detail, and lines that point toward it. A drawing with two competing focal points has none. Everything away from the focal point should be deliberately softer, simpler, and lower-contrast — restraint is the skill.

do: Take one older drawing and identify where your eye actually goes first; if it isn't where you intended, note which tool (contrast, edge, detail) misled it.

children.title: Thumbnails

learn.summary: Thumbnails are tiny (2-8 cm) compositional sketches done in under two minutes each, exploring arrangement and value structure in three or four tones before committing hours to a final. Professionals may thumbnail dozens of options for one illustration. Small size is the point: it forbids detail and forces big-shape decisions.

do: Thumbnail one scene from your home six different ways in under 15 minutes total — vary the crop, angle, and where the darkest dark sits.

children.title: Rule of Thirds & Beyond

learn.summary: Dividing the frame into thirds and placing focal elements on the intersections avoids the static bullseye of dead-center placement — a heuristic first written down by John Thomas Smith in 1797. Related guides: keep the horizon off the middle, and give a moving subject space to move into. These are defaults to break knowingly, not laws.

do: Compose two versions of the same simple scene — subject dead center versus on a thirds intersection — and ask someone which they prefer and why.

children.title: Notan & Value Massing

learn.summary: Notan, from Japanese design tradition, reduces a composition to pure two- or three-value masses of light and dark — no line, no detail. If the design reads powerfully as flat black-and-white shapes, the finished piece will hold together; if not, no rendering will save it. It is the fastest diagnostic for a weak composition.

do: Make two-value notan studies of three photographs or master paintings this week using only a brush pen or marker — every area must commit to black or white.

reflect: Take one drawing you like and crop it three different ways. Which crop is strongest, and why did your first framing miss it?
